beliefs.practice: Read the DocumentDB/Mongo connection URI from an environment variable (DOCUMENTDB_URI) at runtime; never hard-code or commit credentials into source, config files, or logs.

Configure the MongoDB client with sensible connection-pool and timeouts (set maxPoolSize, minPoolSize if available, serverSelectionTimeoutMS, socketTimeoutMS/heartbeatFrequencyMS) to avoid connection storms and long waits during transient network issues.
Always use TLS/SSL for connections to the DocumentDB cluster and validate certificates (do not disable certificate validation in production).
Do not persist OpenAI or DocumentDB API keys in code or committed files; use environment variables or a secrets store (Key Vault, managed identity) and rotate keys periodically.

Use role-based access and least privilege for DB credentials: create a database user with only the minimal privileges needed (read/write on the sample_banking_19 DB and the specific collections) rather than using an admin/root key in the app.

Pick a partitioning/shard key that aligns with query patterns — for per-employee features use a partition key on employee_id (or equivalent) to keep per-employee data co-located and avoid cross-partition scans.

Keep feature documents small and bounded; store embeddings as a separate field (array of floats) and avoid embedding raw logs inside the same document to keep document size under limits and improve read performance.
Use TTL indexes (expireAfterSeconds) for raw activity logs you only need for a retention window, to automatically purge old data and control storage costs.

Create a compound index on (employee_id, timestamp) (or partition key + time) to support efficient queries for recent activity per-employee and to drive aggregation pipelines that compute recent feature vectors.

When storing vector embeddings, ensure the index is created with the correct dimension, metric (cosine/inner/Euclidean), and index type (IVF/HNSW/DiskANN) matching the engine's supported parameters; the stored embedding vectors must match that dimension exactly.

Normalize or standardize embedding vectors consistently (e.g., L2-normalize when using cosine similarity) before persisting and before running nearest-neighbour queries to ensure metric semantics match the index configuration.
Store raw embeddings in a binary-efficient format or as an array of float32 and avoid unnecessary JSON stringification; ensure driver and server preserve numeric precision needed for vector search.
Use bulk/batched writes (bulkWrite or insertMany) when ingesting many feature documents or when seeding logs, and prefer unordered bulk operations for speed where partial failures are acceptable.

Implement idempotent upsert logic for feature documents (use update with upsert:true or replaceOne with upsert) so repeated runs of the ingest or nightly job do not create duplicates or inconsistent state.

Compute centroids and anomaly baselines server-side if possible with aggregation pipelines to reduce network transfer, using $group/$avg, and persist the centroid with metadata (count, last_updated) for efficient nightly comparisons.

When performing nightly checks, process employees in batches and limit concurrency to avoid exhausting client-side connection pool or server RU/throughput; use a resume token/pagination so the job can be safely restarted.
Implement retry logic with exponential backoff for transient errors (network/server selection/timeouts, 429 rate-limited responses), and respect server-provided retry-after headers when present.

When a third-party embedder (OpenAI) is unavailable, persist feature documents without embeddings and flag them for later enrichment; avoid blocking ingestion on successful embedding to preserve pipeline availability.

Monitor and provision throughput appropriately: for Azure DocumentDB / Cosmos-like services, ensure database/collection throughput (RU/s) or autoscale is set to handle peak nightly batch/ingest workloads, and use query metrics and index usage to tune RU consumption.

Add application-level auditing and observability: log high-level operation outcomes (ingest batch sizes, embedding failures, vector index creation), capture query/explain plans for slow queries, and emit metrics/alerts for error rates and latency.
